title: Decorator Pattern
summary: Adding responsibilities to an object at runtime — compression, encryption, logging — by stacking wrappers instead of writing a subclass for every combination.

slides.markdown:
A **Decorator** wraps an object to add new behavior at runtime, while keeping the same interface the rest of the code already expects — so callers can't tell whether they're holding the plain object or ten layers of decoration.

Think of a gift box wrapped in tissue paper, then a ribbon, then a card — each layer adds something without changing the shape of the box underneath. In code, decorators are how `CompressedStream`, `EncryptedStream`, and plain `FileStream` compose freely instead of needing one class per combination.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: adding responsibilities without a subclass explosion
slides.markdown:
Say you have a `Stream` for reading files, and you need variants that compress, encrypt, or both. Subclassing gives you `CompressedStream`, `EncryptedStream`, `CompressedEncryptedStream`, `EncryptedCompressedStream`... every new feature doubles or triples the number of subclasses, and half of them differ only in the order two behaviors are applied.

This is the classic subclass explosion: static inheritance can't express "any combination of these behaviors, chosen at runtime" without enumerating every combination as its own class.

slides.sectionTitle: Decorator: wrap an object, add behavior, preserve the interface
slides.markdown:
The fix: define a decorator that implements the same `Stream` interface and holds a reference to another `Stream` (the thing it wraps). Its `read()` method calls the wrapped stream's `read()` and does its own work on top — decompressing, decrypting, whatever it adds.

Because every decorator and the base object share one interface, you can nest them freely: `EncryptedStream(CompressedStream(FileStream(path)))` gets you both behaviors, in a chosen order, without a single new subclass.

slides.markdown:
![Three concentric rings — EncryptedStream, CompressedStream, and FileStream at the core — with a Client arrow pointing at the outermost ring](assets/decorator-rings.svg)

The client only ever calls the outermost layer. Each layer does its own work, then delegates inward — the core object at the center has no idea it's wrapped.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: layering CompressedStream and EncryptedStream around a base Stream
Compare: Decorator vs inheritance for adding behavior
slides.markdown:
Both add behavior to a base class, but they differ in when the decision is made and how far it scales.

| | Decorator | Inheritance |
|---|---|---|
| When chosen | Runtime — wrap any combination dynamically | Compile time — fixed at the class definition |
| Combinations | Compose freely, no explosion | One subclass per combination needed |
| Coupling | Loose — depends only on the shared interface | Tighter — subclass touches base internals |
| Reversible? | Yes — just don't add the layer | No — baked into the class hierarchy |

**How to decide:** reach for Decorator when behaviors combine differently at runtime; plain inheritance suits one fixed, permanent specialization — this is the same composition-over-inheritance trade-off that shows up everywhere in OOP design.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Decorator vs Proxy — both wrap, but for different reasons
slides.markdown:
Structurally near-identical — both hold a reference to an object implementing the same interface — but their intent diverges completely.

| | Decorator | Proxy |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Add new behavior/responsibility | Control access to the real object |
| Adds features? | Yes — that's the whole point | No — should be behavior-neutral from the caller's view |
| Client awareness | Client deliberately stacks decorators | Client often doesn't know a proxy is there at all |
| Example | Compression, encryption, logging layers | Lazy loading, access control, caching |

**How to decide:** if you're adding something the object couldn't do before, it's Decorator; if you're gatekeeping something it could already do, see [Proxy](proxy-pattern).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: decorator order changing behavior unexpectedly
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Decorators are independent, so wrapping order shouldn't matter."

**Why it's wrong:** `EncryptedStream(CompressedStream(file))` encrypts the compressed bytes; `CompressedStream(EncryptedStream(file))` tries to compress already-encrypted bytes, which barely compresses at all because encrypted data looks like random noise. Same two decorators, same base object, very different — and much worse — outcome.

**Correct model:** decorator order is part of the design, not an implementation detail. Document the required order (compress-then-encrypt, not the reverse) and consider a factory function that assembles the stack correctly, rather than trusting every call site to nest them right.

slides.sectionTitle: Where real libraries use this: I/O stream wrappers, function decorators
slides.markdown:
Java's `BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(...))` and Python's `io` module both use Decorator for exactly this reason — layering buffering, compression, and encoding around a raw byte stream. Python's `@decorator` function syntax is the same idea applied to functions: `@retry` wraps a function so it retries on failure, `@cache` wraps it so results get memoized, and both preserve the original function's call signature.

**When NOT to use it:** if you only ever need one fixed combination of behaviors and it'll never change, a single class with that behavior baked in is simpler to read and debug than an unwinding stack of wrapper objects.
